opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the bar has just become incredibly high. When the transformer came out, it was replacing RNNs and LSTMs, and the improvement was so obvious and so large that people switched almost immediately. You could train faster, it parallelized beautifully on GPUs, and the results were just clearly better. That's what it takes to dislodge an incumbent.

Now the transformer *is* the incumbent, and the whole ecosystem has grown up around it. There are years of engineering in the kernels, things like optimized attention implementations, the hardware is effectively being co-designed for it, the training recipes, the hyperparameter intuitions, the scaling laws, the inference stacks. Everybody knows how to make a transformer work. So if you come along with a new architecture that's, say, a few percent better on some benchmark, that's not enough. People will look at it and say, "Well, I'd have to throw away all this tooling and institutional knowledge, and maybe at scale your advantage disappears anyway." And often they'd be right to be skeptical, because a lot of these improvements don't hold up once you scale them, or once someone tunes the transformer baseline properly.

So I think you need something that's not just slightly better, but obviously, crushingly better, the kind of thing where it'd be foolish not to switch. And I'll be honest, I think that's one of the reasons the field has gotten a bit stuck. There's so much money and attention pouring into one architecture that everyone's doing small variations on it, and there's less room for people to go off and explore genuinely different ideas that might not pay off immediately. Somewhat ironically, as one of the people who worked on it, I'd quite like to see us move past it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says years of transformer tooling, engineering, hardware, and know-how make a small performance gain insufficient; a competitor must be obviously and substantially better to prompt a switch.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes that a competing architecture’s apparent improvements may not hold up at scale and that its advantage may disappear.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I've thought about a lot, partly because I've been on both sides of it. I was one of the people on the transformer paper, and now I run a company that is explicitly trying to get away from it, so I have a sort of personal stake in understanding why it's so sticky.

The thing people underestimate is that an architecture isn't really competing with another architecture. It's competing with an entire ecosystem. When we published "Attention Is All You Need," we got a bit lucky in that the model happened to map incredibly well onto GPUs and TPUs. It's basically all matrix multiplications, it parallelizes beautifully, and so every year since then, the hardware has been optimized for it, the compilers have been optimized for it, the kernels have been hand-tuned for it. Flash attention is a good example. That's not an architectural idea, it's an engineering idea, but it bought transformers a huge amount of headroom that a new architecture doesn't get for free. So when someone shows up with something that's, say, ten or twenty percent better in a fair comparison, it's often not actually ten or twenty percent better in practice, because the transformer is running on a decade of accumulated optimization and the new thing is running on a research codebase.

The second thing is that the comparisons are almost never fair in the way that matters. Most new architectures get evaluated at relatively small scale, because that's what academics can afford, and the transformer has this annoying property that it just keeps working as you scale it. A lot of things that beat transformers at a hundred million parameters either flatten out or get overtaken at ten billion. So the people who could actually afford to test at scale are looking at the paper thinking, "I've seen this story before," and they're not wrong to be skeptical. The burden of proof is enormous, and it's expensive to meet.

And then there's the human side, which I think is actually the biggest factor. The whole field has organized itself around this one thing. Everybody's intuitions are transformer intuitions. The hyperparameters, the learning rate schedules, the tricks you know about initialization, how to debug training when it goes wrong, all of that is tacit knowledge that's been built up around one architecture. If you switch, you throw a lot of that away, and you're back to square one on things that feel like they should be solved. For a lab that's got a model to ship in six months, that's not an attractive trade, even if the thing is genuinely better.

What I find a little sad about it, honestly, is that it's made the field quite conservative. There's been so much money flowing into scaling the thing that works that there's very little incentive to actually explore. I say this half as a joke, but I think the transformer being so good has in some ways been bad for research, because it became the safe bet and the field collapsed onto it. That's a big part of why we started Sakana. We wanted to be in a position where we could afford to be curious about alternatives without needing them to immediately win on the standard benchmarks.

So my honest answer is that "performs better" is doing a lot of work in that question. Better on what, at what scale, on what hardware, with how many years of tuning behind it? Until a new architecture is better across all of those at once, or offers something transformers fundamentally can't do rather than just doing the same thing slightly more efficiently, I think the inertia wins. The way it eventually gets displaced is probably not by something that's a bit better at language modeling. It's by something that opens up a capability people actually want and can't get any other way.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers benefit from years of hardware, compiler, and kernel optimization, so a new architecture’s apparent advantage may not hold in practice and the burden to displace them is high.

r002.rationale: It observes that alternatives beating transformers at small scale may flatten out or be overtaken at ten billion parameters as transformers continue to scale.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a huge amount of inertia. You’re not just competing with the transformer as an architecture; you’re competing with all the work that’s gone into making it run well. The hardware, the kernels, the training recipes—people have spent years figuring those things out.

So you might have a better idea, but your first implementation is competing against a very mature implementation of the transformer. And if it’s only a little bit better on some benchmark, that may not be enough to persuade someone to rebuild their infrastructure around it.

There’s also the question of scale. Something can look really promising in a small experiment, but somebody has to take the risk of spending a lot of compute to find out whether that advantage survives. With transformers, people have a much clearer idea of what they’re going to get. So a replacement needs more than a good result; it needs a convincing reason to make that switch.

r001.rationale: The response describes the transformer’s mature ecosystem—hardware, kernels, training recipes, and infrastructure—and says a small performance gain may not justify switching. This communicates that the competitor needs a larger advantage to displace it.

r002.rationale: The response says an advantage seen in a small experiment may not survive spending more compute, but does not state that scaling up a transformer can erase a competing architecture’s advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a big difference between having a better result and having something that people are willing to switch to. You’re not just competing with the transformer as an architecture. You’re competing with all the infrastructure around it—the optimized kernels, the training recipes, the experience people have debugging it.

So if your new architecture is a little bit better on some benchmark, that might not compensate for the cost and risk of moving everything over. And people will reasonably ask: does it still work at a much larger scale? Does it work across all the tasks we care about? Can we train it reliably?

That creates a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem. Transformers get a lot of investment because people use them, and people use them because they’ve had a lot of investment. To break through that, I think you need either a really substantial improvement or a particular setting where the advantage is clear enough that switching becomes worthwhile.

r001.rationale: It says a new architecture’s benchmark improvement may not offset the cost and risk of switching from transformers’ surrounding infrastructure, and that a substantial improvement may be needed to make switching worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the new architecture works at a much larger scale, but does not say that scaling up a transformer could erase the competing architecture’s advantage.
